transcript.text: Every so often when I put the washing machine on the whole kitchen power goes off and I have to go to the fuse box and flick the switch back up. It doesn't happen every time. Indesit, IWE 7 something.

That sounds like the washing machine is intermittently tripping either:

• An RCD/RCBO – usually indicates earth leakage, often from a failing heating element, motor, pump, wiring, or moisture inside the machine.
• A circuit breaker/MCB – more likely a short circuit or overload on the kitchen socket circuit.

Because it is not every wash, a common pattern is that it trips when the machine starts heating the water (often 10–30 minutes into a cycle), which can point to a deteriorating heating element. Drain/spin-related trips can point more towards the pump or motor.

### What to do now
1. Avoid repeatedly resetting the switch and carrying on, especially if it trips again. That protection is operating for a reason.
2. Unplug the washer before checking anything externally.
3. Check for obvious issues:
• Water underneath or behind the machine
• Damaged plug, cable, or socket
• Signs of burning, heat, looseness, or discolouration at the plug/socket
• Machine plugged into an extension lead or adaptor — don’t use one for a washing machine.
4. If practical, try the machine on its own with other high-load kitchen appliances off (kettle, oven, dishwasher, tumble dryer etc.). This may distinguish an overloaded circuit from a washer fault — but stop if it trips again.
5. Note when it trips: immediately on switching on, when it fills, during heating, while draining, or on spin. That is useful for an appliance engineer.

### Best next step
Have an appliance engineer inspect the Indesit, or an electrician if there are concerns about the socket/circuit. Tell them that it intermittently trips the kitchen circuit and at what stage it happens. Heating elements are a fairly common repair, but it needs proper testing rather than guesswork.

If the breaker trips even with the washer unplugged, or the socket is hot/burnt, there is water near electrics, or you smell burning, leave that circuit off and call an electrician.

Thanks, I've been keeping notes so I can answer most of that. It does trip with the kettle and dishwasher off, so it's only the washing machine running. The plug looks fine, not warm and no marks on it. The floor is dry, though I haven't looked inside the machine. There's no burning smell and I haven't seen any sparking.

On timing, it always trips a few minutes into a 40 or 60 degree wash. It has never tripped on a cold wash or on rinse and spin. I'll be honest that I've been resetting the switch each time and carrying on, since it only happens about 1 in 4 washes. Is that a problem?

Yes — that pattern strongly points to a fault in the washer’s heating circuit, most commonly a heating element beginning to leak current to earth as it warms up.

The fact that it:

• happens only on 40/60 °C washes,
• occurs a few minutes in,
• does not happen on cold washes or rinse/spin, and
• happens with other kitchen appliances off,

makes an overloaded kitchen circuit very unlikely.

Resetting the switch once after an unexplained trip is reasonable; repeatedly resetting it and continuing to use the appliance is not a good idea. The device is likely an RCD/RCBO and is disconnecting power because it detects electricity potentially going somewhere it should not — possibly through the machine casing or an earth path. It may be intermittent now, but faults of this type can worsen.

### What I’d do
• Stop using heated programmes and, ideally, stop using the machine altogether until it has been checked.
• Unplug it when not in use.
• Arrange an appliance repair engineer and describe it as:
  “Indesit IWE 7… intermittently trips the RCD/consumer-unit switch a few minutes into 40 °C and 60 °C programmes, but cold wash and rinse/spin are OK.”
• Ask them to test the heating element and wiring for insulation/earth leakage. A heater element is often a replaceable repair, rather than meaning the whole machine is beyond repair.

A cold cycle not tripping is useful evidence, but it does not prove the machine is completely safe to keep using: there can still be dampness, damaged insulation, or a loose connection which changes as the machine vibrates or heats.

Do not remove panels or try to test it live yourself. If it starts tripping immediately when plugged in, you get a tingling sensation from the case/taps, notice water, smell burning, or the plug/socket becomes warm, leave it unplugged and seek prompt help.
